items.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
items.summary:
How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude. At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important.
Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.

items.summary:
If you use Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, Cursor, or VS Code Copilot with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, your context window and prompt cache are exposed to three silent failure modes:
- 
Startup Schema Bloat (tools/list): Connecting 3 common MCP servers (github, postgres, playwright) injects 60+ tool JSON schemas (~20,000+ tokens) into every single turn.

items.summary: My mind is all always all over the place (ADD?) and often I would have ideas I wanted to test/implement while I was on the go/on my phone. I was frustrated that the available solutions (claude --cloud or /remote-control) seemed to split sessions across devices and/or not let me iterate directly on the project I wanted to work on. Using a spare laptop I essentially built a "claude code server": * Carry your Claude Code sessions across all your devices. * An always-on machine at home (the "box") runs your Claude Code sessions. * Your laptop opens them over SSH, your phone through the Claude app, and you can switch between them mid-conversation: start on the laptop, carry on from the phone, finish on the laptop. items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.summary:
16th November 2026
A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.
Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code.
Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:
select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))
Returns this:
{"a":[1]}
But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:
{"a":"[1]"}
According to D. Richard Hipp:
That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.
The workaround looks like this:
select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))
